patient.name: Desmond Clarke
patient.complaint: Three months of looser, more frequent stools with dark blood mixed in
background: Prostate cancer treated with external beam radiotherapy 8 years ago

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with an older patient, change in bowel habit, bleeding, weight loss or iron-deficiency anaemia; the side (right vs left) and family history (Lynch, FAP) are the twists.

points: Desmond, 69, three months of **looser, more frequent stools**.
Dark blood **mixed in** with the stool, not just on the paper.
Crampy left lower abdominal pain; trousers looser: **lost 6 kg**.
Feels he has not finished after opening his bowels.

steps.lead: An older man with a new change in bowel habit and blood: think **colorectal adenocarcinoma**, the end point of the adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence.
Desmond stacks up risk factors: **age**, prior **pelvic radiotherapy** for prostate cancer, smoking, obesity and a low-fibre diet.

points: Firm, non-tender **mass in the left iliac fossa**.
DRE: no rectal mass; dark blood on the glove.

visual.title: Where Desmond's mass is
visual.caption: LIF mass with bleeding and altered habit points to a **left-sided (sigmoid)** tumour; a RIF mass with anaemia suggests caecal.

steps.lead: Bleeding, altered habit, colicky pain and an **LIF mass** place Desmond's tumour on the **left**. A caecal cancer would more likely hide as anaemia alone.

steps.q: Which single feature most strongly suggests Desmond's tumour is left-sided?
o: Change in bowel habit with LIF mass
steps.r: Left-sided tumours narrow a solid-stool lumen, so they change bowel habit early. Anaemia, a RIF mass and weight loss alone suggest **right-sided** disease.

steps.lead: Desmond has no family history, so this looks sporadic. A young patient with relatives with bowel or endometrial cancer should make you think **Lynch** (3-2-1 rule).

steps.text: **Lynch** = right-sided, young, mismatch repair genes, endometrial cancer in the family. **FAP** = hundreds of polyps, APC. **Peutz-Jeghers** = lip freckles plus hamartomas.

steps.lead: Once resected, Desmond's tumour will be given a **Duke's stage**: A and B have no nodes, C has nodes, D has distant metastases.

steps.text: Do not blame bleeding in a 69 year old on haemorrhoids. **Dark blood mixed with stool** plus weight loss is cancer until colonoscopy says otherwise.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (FIT in primary care) or 'diagnostic investigation?' (colonoscopy with biopsy); CT colonography is the fallback and CT CAP/MRI pelvis stage.

steps.title: Desmond's GP bloods
steps.text: Microcytic, iron-deficiency anaemia with a strongly positive FIT.

steps.lead: Desmond's GP sends a **FIT**: at **142 µg/g** it is far above the **10** cut-off, so he goes on the **2-week-wait** pathway for colonoscopy.

visual.title: FIT result (µg Hb per g faeces)
visual.label: Desmond 142
visual.caption: Anything **≥10 µg/g** triggers an urgent suspected-cancer referral.

steps.r: **Colonoscopy with biopsy** is gold standard: it sees the lesion and gives histology. FIT and CEA cannot diagnose; CT colonography cannot biopsy.

steps.lead: Colonoscopy shows an ulcerating, **stricturing sigmoid** lesion at 25 cm; biopsies confirm **adenocarcinoma** and a small polyp is removed.
Had the scope not passed the stricture, **CT colonography** would image the rest of the colon. His **LFTs** are normal, which is reassuring about liver spread.

steps.title: Suspected colorectal cancer pathway
nodes: Symptoms or anaemia in primary care
CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (± MRI pelvis if rectal)
steps.caption: Screen, confirm, then stage.

steps.lead: Desmond's **CT CAP** shows no liver or lung metastases; baseline **CEA** is taken to track his treatment. MRI pelvis would be needed if this were **rectal**.

steps.text: **CEA** is for monitoring treatment and recurrence, not for diagnosing or screening.
**NHS screening**: FIT every **2 years, ages 50 to 74**. Desmond had stopped returning his kits.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate definitive management?' where the tumour site picks the operation, or an emergency vignette (obstruction, perforation, anastomotic leak).

steps.lead: The small polyp found at Desmond's colonoscopy was removed there and then: **polypectomy** is first-line for benign or pre-malignant polyps.

steps.q: Desmond's tumour is in the sigmoid colon, with no metastases. Which operation?
steps.r: A sigmoid tumour needs a **sigmoid colectomy / high anterior resection**. AP resection is for low rectal tumours; hemicolectomies for more proximal sites.

steps.lead: Desmond has an elective **high anterior resection** with primary anastomosis; the MDT plans adjuvant chemotherapy if nodes are positive.
An **epidural** helps Desmond's bowels start working sooner after surgery. If he had metastases, oncology would lead with palliative chemo or a stent.

points: Day 6 after surgery: new abdominal pain and fever.
He is muddled overnight and his bowels have stopped again.

steps.q: What is the most likely cause of Desmond's deterioration?
steps.r: Days **5 to 7**, pain, fever, delirium, prolonged ileus and sepsis is an **anastomotic leak** until proven otherwise.

steps.lead: Desmond is septic, so he has a **CT abdomen/pelvis** first, then **IV antibiotics** and an **exploratory laparotomy**. In an emergency, an **end colostomy** (Hartmann's) is safer than re-joining.

visual.title: Desmond after surgery
visual.caption: CRP should fall after day 3; a **second rise around day 5 to 7** with tachycardia is the leak signal.

steps.lead: Desmond's journey follows the **NICE 2-week-wait** criteria, **Duke's** staging of his specimen and the **FIT** screening programme.

steps.text: A primary anastomosis is the wrong answer in a **perforated or obstructed** emergency: **Hartmann's** with end colostomy is the safe choice.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: which gene starts the adenoma-carcinoma sequence (APC), how Lynch differs (mismatch repair, microsatellite instability), or why right-sided tumours present with anaemia.

steps.lead: Desmond's cancer probably began as a polyp years ago: **APC** loss first, then **KRAS**, then **p53**.

steps.title: Adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence
steps.caption: Removing polyps breaks the chain, which is why screening works.

steps.lead: A younger patient with **Lynch** skips much of this: faulty **mismatch repair** causes microsatellite instability and fast right-sided cancers.

steps.q: Which gene is mutated in FAP?
steps.r: **APC** (tumour suppressor) in FAP. MLH1 is Lynch; STK11 is Peutz-Jeghers; KRAS is a later step.

steps.lead: Desmond's sigmoid tumour grew **circumferentially** in a narrow, solid-stool lumen, so he noticed his bowel habit change early.
Desmond's CT checked his **liver** first because colonic venous blood drains through the **portal vein**.

visual.title: Duke's stage of Desmond's specimen
visual.label: Desmond C1
visual.caption: Two nodes positive, apical node clear: **Duke's C1**, about 40% 5-year survival.

mcq.q: What is the most common cause of large bowel obstruction?
mcq.r: **Colorectal cancer**; adhesions are the commonest cause of small bowel obstruction.

mcq.q: Which presentation fits a caecal cancer best?
mcq.r: Right-sided tumours bleed occultly: **iron-deficiency anaemia** and a RIF mass.

mcq.q: Lynch syndrome is caused by mutations in which genes?
Which Duke's stage has regional lymph node involvement without distant metastases?
What FIT result triggers a 2-week-wait referral?
What is the gold-standard diagnostic test for colorectal cancer?
What does the NHS bowel screening programme offer?
Which operation treats a rectal tumour 4 cm from the anal verge?
mcq.r: Within **8 cm**: AP resection with permanent end colostomy.

mcq.q: When does an anastomotic leak typically present?
Which is the early initiating mutation in most sporadic colorectal cancers?
mcq.r: **APC** loss is first; KRAS and p53 come later.

prompts.q: How does right-sided colon cancer present compared with left-sided and rectal cancer?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the side changes the vignette.

points.p: Right: iron-deficiency anaemia, weight loss, RIF mass, late
points.why: No bowel symptoms in an anaemic elderly patient = caecal.

points.p: Left: rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit, colicky pain, obstruction, LIF mass
Rectal: bleeding, tenesmus, incomplete emptying

prompts.q: What are the risk factors for colorectal cancer?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: look for the hidden family history or radiotherapy.

points.p: Adenomatous polyps, Lynch, FAP, IBD
Increasing age; prior pelvic radiotherapy (prostate)
points.why: External beam radiotherapy for prostate cancer is in the notes.

points.p: Smoking, obesity, low-fibre diet

prompts.q: How do you tell Lynch syndrome, FAP, Gardner's and Peutz-Jeghers apart?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: polyp number and extra-colonic clues.

points.p: Lynch: MLH1/MSH2 mismatch repair, AD, right-sided, endometrial/ovarian cancer
3-2-1 rule: 3 relatives, 2 generations, 1 under 50
points.why: Plus at least one first-degree relative.

points.p: FAP: APC, hundreds of polyps; Gardner's adds osteomas, cysts, extra teeth
Peutz-Jeghers: hamartomas plus pigmented lips, palms, soles
points.why: Raised gastric cancer risk; conservative management.

prompts.q: Outline Duke's staging A to D.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: nodes make it C, metastases make it D.

points.p: A: confined beneath muscularis propria
B: through muscularis propria, no nodes
C: nodes involved (C1 apical clear, C2 apical involved)
D: distant metastases

prompts.q: What complications can a colorectal tumour cause?

points.p: Large bowel obstruction
Liver metastases
Perforation, anaemia, cachexia

prompts.q: What is the first-line test in primary care, its cut-off, and who gets referred urgently?

points.p: FIT; ≥10 µg Hb/g → 2-week-wait colonoscopy
≥40 with unexplained weight loss and abdominal pain
≥50 with rectal bleeding, pain or weight loss; ≥60 with anaemia
points.why: Also abdominal mass, change in bowel habit, IDA.

prompts.q: What confirms colorectal cancer, what is the fallback, and how is it staged and monitored?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: diagnose, then stage, then monitor.

points.p: Colonoscopy and biopsy (gold standard)
CT colonography if colonoscopy fails
CT chest/abdomen/pelvis; MRI pelvis for rectal
CEA to monitor; screening FIT 2-yearly at 50–74

prompts.q: Which operation for each tumour site?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the site picks the operation.

points.p: Caecum/ascending/proximal transverse: right hemicolectomy
Distal transverse/descending: left hemicolectomy
Sigmoid: sigmoid colectomy / high anterior resection
Rectum >8 cm: anterior resection + loop ileostomy; within 8 cm: AP resection
FAP: total proctocolectomy with ileal pouch; polyps: polypectomy

prompts.q: How do you manage colorectal cancer emergencies and an anastomotic leak?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: never join bowel in a septic emergency.

points.p: Obstructing/perforated sigmoid: Hartmann's (end colostomy)
Stage IV obstruction: palliative stent
Leak at days 5–7: pain, fever, delirium, ileus, sepsis
Gastrografin enema or CT; IV antibiotics and laparotomy

prompts.q: Describe the adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence and how Lynch differs.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the genes in order.

points.p: APC loss first (tumour suppressor)
Then KRAS, then p53
points.why: Takes years, so polypectomy prevents cancer.

points.p: Lynch: mismatch repair failure → microsatellite instability, fast, right-sided

prompts.q: Why do right- and left-sided tumours present differently?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: lumen size and stool consistency.

points.p: Right: wide lumen, liquid stool, exophytic growth → occult bleeding, anaemia
Left: narrow lumen, solid stool, napkin-ring growth → obstruction, habit change

glossary.adenocarcinoma: Cancer arising from glandular epithelium; over 90% of colorectal cancers.
glossary.adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence: Stepwise mutations turning a benign adenomatous polyp into invasive cancer over years.
glossary.adenomatous polyp: A benign, pre-malignant growth of colonic glandular tissue.
glossary.Lynch syndrome: Autosomal dominant mismatch repair defect causing early right-sided colorectal and endometrial cancers.
glossary.HNPCC: Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer; another name for Lynch syndrome.
glossary.FAP: Familial adenomatous polyposis: APC mutation causing hundreds of colonic polyps and near-certain cancer.
glossary.Gardner's: FAP variant with osteomas, epidermoid cysts, lipomas and supernumerary teeth.
glossary.Peutz-Jeghers syndrome: Autosomal dominant hamartomatous GI polyps with dark freckles on lips, palms and soles.
glossary.hamartomatous: Made of a disorganised overgrowth of normal tissue, not true neoplasia.
glossary.APC: Tumour suppressor gene whose loss starts the adenoma-carcinoma sequence.
glossary.KRAS: Oncogene mutated midway through the adenoma-carcinoma sequence.
glossary.p53: Tumour suppressor lost late, as an adenoma becomes a carcinoma.
glossary.MLH1: DNA mismatch repair gene mutated in Lynch syndrome.
glossary.MSH2: DNA mismatch repair gene mutated in Lynch syndrome.
glossary.microsatellite instability: Changes in length of repetitive DNA sequences when mismatch repair fails.
glossary.mismatch repair: The system that corrects copying errors in DNA; faulty in Lynch syndrome.
glossary.3-2-1 rule: Lynch screen: 3 relatives, 2 generations, 1 diagnosed under 50.
glossary.tenesmus: A constant feeling of needing to open the bowels even when the rectum is empty.
glossary.occult bleeding: Blood loss not visible to the eye, found by tests or as anaemia.
glossary.muscularis propria: The main muscle layer of the bowel wall; key landmark in Duke's staging.
glossary.Duke's: Colorectal cancer staging A to D based on wall invasion, nodes and metastases.
glossary.apical node: The highest lymph node at the vascular tie; its involvement makes Duke's C2.
glossary.FIT: Faecal immunochemical test; measures human haemoglobin in stool.
glossary.2-week-wait: NHS urgent suspected-cancer referral, seen within two weeks.
glossary.colonoscopy: Camera examination of the whole colon allowing biopsy and polyp removal.
glossary.CT colonography: CT 'virtual colonoscopy' after bowel preparation and gas insufflation.
glossary.CEA: Carcinoembryonic antigen; tumour marker used to monitor colorectal cancer treatment.
glossary.right hemicolectomy: Removal of caecum, ascending and proximal transverse colon.
glossary.left hemicolectomy: Removal of distal transverse and descending colon.
glossary.anterior resection: Removal of the upper rectum with anastomosis, often protected by a loop ileostomy.
glossary.abdomino-perineal resection: Removal of rectum, anal canal and anus, leaving a permanent end colostomy.
glossary.Hartmann's procedure: Sigmoid colectomy with end colostomy and closed rectal stump; used in emergencies.
glossary.end colostomy: The cut end of the colon brought out on the abdomen as a stoma.
glossary.loop ileostomy: A loop of ileum opened on the skin to divert stool, usually temporarily.
glossary.anastomosis: A surgical join between two ends of bowel.
glossary.anastomotic leak: Leakage of bowel contents from a surgical join, typically days 5 to 7.
glossary.ileus: Temporary paralysis of bowel movement without a mechanical block.
glossary.gastrografin: Water-soluble contrast used to look for leaks.
glossary.neoadjuvant: Treatment such as radiotherapy given before surgery to shrink a tumour.
glossary.proctocolectomy: Removal of the entire colon and rectum.
glossary.ileal pouch: A reservoir made from ileum joined to the anus after proctocolectomy.
glossary.napkin-ring: A tumour growing all the way round the bowel, narrowing it.
glossary.cachexia: Wasting of muscle and fat from chronic disease such as cancer.
glossary.portal vein: Carries blood from the gut to the liver; why colorectal cancer spreads to the liver first.
glossary.epidural: Local anaesthetic infusion around the spinal cord; speeds bowel recovery after surgery.

technique.stem: A 72 year old woman has a 4 month history of tiredness and breathlessness on exertion. She has lost 5 kg in weight. Her bowel habit is unchanged and she has not noticed any rectal bleeding. On examination she is pale and there is a firm mass in the right iliac fossa.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question in an older woman with symptoms of anaemia: think about where occult blood loss comes from.

clues: mass in the right iliac fossa
steps.x: Anaemia symptoms + weight loss + **no change in habit or visible blood** + **RIF mass** = right-sided tumour.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Right-sided colon cancer: **caecal carcinoma**.

elim: No fever, pain or acute onset; this is months of weight loss.
Unusual new presentation at 72; expect diarrhoea, pain and raised inflammatory markers.
Rectal cancer gives bleeding and tenesmus, not a RIF mass with silent anaemia.
Left-sided tumours change bowel habit and bleed visibly; mass would be LIF.

steps.x: **B. Caecal carcinoma.** Right side = anaemia + RIF mass, presents late.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man sees his GP with a 6 week history of looser stools and intermittent left lower abdominal pain. He has lost 3 kg in weight. Abdominal examination and rectal examination are normal.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

steps.x: Initial investigation in primary care for possible colorectal cancer: think of the triage test that decides referral.

clues: examination and rectal examination are normal
steps.x: Over 60 with change in bowel habit and weight loss, no mass: NICE says **FIT** first.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **FIT**: if ≥10 µg/g, 2-week-wait colonoscopy.

elim: A monitoring marker, not a diagnostic or triage test.
Second-line, used when colonoscopy fails or is unsuitable.
Distinguishes IBD from IBS in younger patients; not the cancer triage test.
Not the primary care first step; misses proximal disease.

steps.x: **D. Faecal immunochemical test.** In primary care, FIT is the initial test; colonoscopy is the diagnostic one.

technique.stem: A 63 year old man has a biopsy-proven adenocarcinoma of the rectum. MRI pelvis shows the tumour is 4 cm from the anal verge and involves the anal sphincter. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no metastases.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive surgical management?

steps.x: Definitive surgery: the tumour's distance from the anal verge chooses the operation.
Low rectal tumour within 8 cm, sphincter involved, curable: remove rectum and anus.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **AP resection** with a permanent end colostomy.

elim: For tumours **more than 8 cm** from the anal verge.
An emergency operation for perforation or obstruction.
For descending colon tumours, not the rectum.
For FAP, not a single sporadic tumour.

steps.x: **A. Abdomino-perineal resection.** Within 8 cm = APR; above 8 cm = anterior resection.

technique.stem: A 34 year old woman has a right-sided colonic adenocarcinoma. Her mother had endometrial cancer at 48 and her maternal uncle had colon cancer at 55. Tumour testing shows microsatellite instability.
technique.q: Which is the most likely underlying mechanism?

steps.x: A mechanism question: what process has failed?
Young, right-sided, family endometrial and colon cancers, MSI: **Lynch syndrome**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Lynch = germline **mismatch repair** defect (MLH1/MSH2).

elim: A later step in the sporadic adenoma-carcinoma sequence.
FAP: hundreds of polyps, not microsatellite instability.
Peutz-Jeghers: hamartomas and mucocutaneous pigmentation.
Late event in sporadic cancer; does not explain MSI.

steps.x: **B. Defective DNA mismatch repair.** MSI is the fingerprint of mismatch repair failure.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has a 2 month history of passing looser stools more often, with dark blood mixed in. He has lost 4 kg. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 140/86 mmHg. There is a firm mass in the left iliac fossa.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Altered habit, blood mixed with stool, weight loss and an LIF mass in a 70 year old is sigmoid cancer. Diverticulitis is acute and febrile.

steps.x: Diagnosis: older man, altered habit, blood, weight loss.

clues: mass in the left iliac fossa
steps.x: Change in bowel habit + mixed blood + weight loss + LIF mass = left-sided cancer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sigmoid carcinoma.**

elim: Acute LIF pain with fever; he is afebrile with a 2 month history.
Bright red blood on the paper, no weight loss, no mass.
Sudden pain and bloody diarrhoea in a vasculopath.
Bloody diarrhoea with urgency, usually younger; no mass.

steps.x: **D. Sigmoid carcinoma.** Left-sided cancer changes bowel habit and bleeds visibly.

practice.stem: A 78 year old woman is referred with fatigue. She has no gastrointestinal symptoms. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 128/74 mmHg. She is pale and has a mass in the right iliac fossa.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Microcytic anaemia with a RIF mass and no bowel symptoms is classic right-sided (caecal) cancer from occult bleeding.

steps.x: Diagnosis: anaemia with no bowel symptoms.

clues: mass in the right iliac fossa
steps.x: Silent iron-deficiency anaemia + RIF mass = right-sided cancer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Caecal carcinoma.**

elim: Does not cause a RIF mass; usually diarrhoea or bloating.
Epigastric symptoms and mass, early satiety.
Pelvic mass with bloating; does not explain iron deficiency.
Bleeding and tenesmus, mass on DRE.

steps.x: **A. Caecal carcinoma.** Right-sided tumours present late with anaemia.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man has a 3 day history of colicky abdominal pain, abdominal distension and vomiting. He has not passed stool or flatus for 2 days. For 3 months his bowels had become increasingly constipated. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. The abdomen is distended and tympanic.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause?
practice.e: Colorectal cancer is the most common cause of large bowel obstruction; the preceding change in bowel habit gives it away.

steps.x: Most likely cause of large bowel obstruction.
Months of change in habit leading to absolute constipation: an obstructing left-sided tumour.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Colorectal carcinoma.**

elim: Small bowel cause; he has no previous surgery.
Would not cause absolute constipation, vomiting and progressive months of change.
Follows surgery or electrolyte upset; pain is not colicky.
Needs a tender irreducible groin lump.

steps.x: **B. Colorectal carcinoma.** Commonest cause of large bowel obstruction.

practice.stem: A 38 year old man has a right-sided colon cancer. His father had colon cancer at 46 and his paternal aunt had endometrial cancer at 52. Colonoscopy shows only one or two polyps.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Young right-sided cancer with relatives with colon and endometrial cancer meets the 3-2-1 rule for Lynch; FAP has hundreds of polyps.

steps.x: Diagnosis: young cancer plus family history.
3 relatives, 2 generations, 1 under 50, right-sided, few polyps: **3-2-1 rule** fits.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lynch syndrome (HNPCC).**

elim: Hundreds to thousands of polyps, not one or two.
FAP variant with osteomas, cysts and extra teeth.
Multiple hamartomas in childhood, no endometrial link.
Hamartomas and pigmented lip lesions.

steps.x: **D. Lynch syndrome.** Few polyps + endometrial cancer in family = Lynch.

practice.stem: A 19 year old woman has a colonoscopy because her mother had a colectomy at 30. Hundreds of adenomatous polyps carpet the colon. She also has an osteoma of the jaw, several epidermoid cysts and a supernumerary tooth.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Hundreds of adenomas means FAP; osteomas, epidermoid cysts and supernumerary teeth make it Gardner's variant.

steps.x: Diagnosis: polyposis plus extra-colonic signs.
FAP (APC) plus osteomas, epidermoid cysts and extra teeth: Gardner's variant.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Gardner's syndrome.**

elim: Hamartomas, macrocephaly and breast/thyroid cancer.
Few polyps; extracolonic cancers are endometrial and ovarian.
Hamartomas with pigmented lips; not hundreds of adenomas.
Polyposis with brain tumours.

steps.x: **B. Gardner's syndrome.** FAP + bones, cysts, teeth = Gardner's.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man has a sigmoid colectomy for adenocarcinoma. Histology shows tumour invading through the muscularis propria with 3 of 14 regional lymph nodes involved; the apical node is clear. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no metastases.
practice.e: Nodal involvement without metastases is Duke's C, and a clear apical node makes it C1.

steps.x: A staging question: walk through wall, nodes, apical node, metastases.
Nodes positive, no metastases = C; apical node clear = C1.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Confined beneath the muscularis propria, no nodes.
Through muscularis propria but node-negative.
Requires the **apical node** to be involved.
Requires distant metastases.

steps.x: **C. C1.** C1 apical clear (~40% 5-year survival); C2 apical involved.

practice.stem: A 71 year old woman has a 2 month history of change in bowel habit. Colonoscopy could not pass a tight stricture at 30 cm and biopsies are awaited. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 136/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation to assess the rest of the colon?
practice.e: When colonoscopy is incomplete, CT colonography assesses the remaining colon and can pick up liver metastases.

steps.x: Next investigation when colonoscopy has failed.

clues: Colonoscopy could not pass a tight stricture
steps.x: Incomplete colonoscopy: **CT colonography** images the proximal colon and can show liver metastases.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT colonography.**

elim: Images the oesophagus, not the colon.
For small bowel; risks retention at a stricture.
Already past triage; it cannot image the colon.
Shows obstruction, not mucosal lesions.

steps.x: **B. CT colonography.** Colonoscopy failed → CT colonography.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man had a right hemicolectomy for Duke's B caecal adenocarcinoma 1 year ago. He is well. He attends follow-up.
practice.q: Which blood test is most appropriate to monitor for recurrence?
practice.e: CEA is the colorectal tumour marker used for monitoring treatment response and recurrence.

steps.x: Tumour marker for colorectal follow-up.
Colorectal cancer follow-up marker: **CEA**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Carcinoembryonic antigen.**

elim: Hepatocellular carcinoma and germ cell tumours.
Mainly pancreatic and biliary cancer.
Ovarian cancer.
Prostate cancer.

steps.x: **D. Carcinoembryonic antigen.** CEA monitors response and recurrence, never diagnoses.

practice.stem: A 68 year old woman has an adenocarcinoma in the ascending colon on colonoscopy and biopsy. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no metastases. She is otherwise fit.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
practice.e: Caecal, ascending and proximal transverse tumours are treated with a right hemicolectomy.

steps.x: Definitive surgery: match site to operation.
Caecum, ascending or proximal transverse: right hemicolectomy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Right hemicolectomy.**

elim: For low rectal tumours.
For benign or pre-malignant polyps, not invasive cancer.
For distal transverse and descending tumours.
For stage IV obstruction; she is curable.

steps.x: **E. Right hemicolectomy.** Right-sided tumours = right hemicolectomy, usually primary anastomosis.

practice.stem: A 79 year old man with a known sigmoid tumour has a 2 day history of distension, vomiting and absolute constipation. CT shows a perforation proximal to the tumour with free fluid. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 122 bpm and BP 92/58 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate operation?
practice.e: Hartmann's procedure (sigmoid colectomy with end colostomy) avoids an anastomosis in a contaminated, septic abdomen.

steps.x: Emergency operation for a perforated, obstructing sigmoid tumour.
Septic perforation: resect and do not join; bring out an end colostomy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hartmann's procedure.**

elim: For low rectal cancer, elective.
For stage IV obstruction without perforation.
Wrong side.
High leak risk in a septic, perforated patient.

steps.x: **C. Hartmann's procedure.** Emergency + sigmoid = Hartmann's.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man is 6 days after an anterior resection for rectal cancer. He develops abdominal pain, fever and new confusion and has not opened his bowels. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 120 bpm and BP 90/56 mmHg. He has peritonism.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management after resuscitation and imaging?
practice.e: An anastomotic leak with peritonitis and shock is treated with IV antibiotics and exploratory laparotomy, usually with a stoma.

steps.x: Management of a post-operative complication.
Day 6, septic, peritonitic: anastomotic leak needs IV antibiotics and laparotomy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV antibiotics and laparotomy.**

elim: Treats ileus; he is septic and peritonitic.
Decompression does not control sepsis.
Too little for septic shock.
